newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bank payment market set for shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Australian bank payment market set for shake-up.

text.p: Australia's plan to open the nation's payments system is seen opening the way for foreign financial giants, telecom groups and retailers into what had been a cosy market, analysts said on Thursday.

The Australian government commissioned Wallis Inquiry into the local financial industry recommended on Wednesday that the payment system be open to non-banks and is seen as the key to further competition in the financial services industry.

Australian banking analysts said they expect overseas financial conglomerates like GE Capital and American Express, along with the nation's largest retailer Coles Myer Ltd to become bigger players in the payments system.
The payment system is the physical infrastructure that allows people and corporations to transfer money from one party to another, either by cheque, electronically or by credit card.

"You are looking at merchant banks, Merrill Lynch and SBC for example," said Jeremy Pooley a banking and finance partner at accountants Coppers and Lybrand on being asked what companies would be entering the Australian payments market.
U.S.-based investment bank Merrill Lynch and Swiss finance giant Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) are both major players in Australia's investment markets.

"The electronic payments system was opened up to the building societies and credit unions last year and now the way is clearly open for insurance companies and the likes of Lend Lease's of the world," said Vic Edwards director of National Centre for Banking at University of New South Wales (NSW).
Australian finance and property group Lend Lease Corp Ltd already operates payroll services.

"I would imagine Coles Myer particularly with its tie-up with ANZ, might see that it is also in an ideal postion," Edwards told Reuters. Australia and New Zealand Banking Group (ANZ) has bank facilities at Coles Myer supermarkets.
State-owned Australia Post and telephone group Telstra Corp were also seen as other players to become more involved in Australia's financial services market, Edwards said.
Australia Post is an agent for four local banks, while Telstra is enjoying strong growth from the increasing popularity of telephone banking.

The Wallis report recommended changes to the payment system mainly due to the introduction of technology, such as electronic funds transfer, smart cards, Internet and the growth in Automatic Teller Machines (ATM), along with loyality programmes.

The introduction of electronic systems like Mondex and a secure Internet payments system will have a profound effect on the market, analysts said. Mondex, known as an electronic purse, allows the transfer of value from one card to another.
However, analysts said to enter the payment system will not be a free for all. "There are some concerns about who you let into the system," said Pooley from Coopers and Lybrand.
"It may be difficult for an institution without a track record and without a network here," said Edwards.

The Wallis recommendations are seen to carry Australia's banking industry into the next century, but technology may overtake these new rules in another few decades, said Andrew Willink director of banking products research group Cannex.
"The thing that is going to make a difference is whether people have a intelligent chip on their (smart) card or not, so they can use funds whenever and wherever they can," he said.
